title: Four billion times better
caption: The Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Milky Way stretches over ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory, in Chile's remote Atacama Desert. The sky is filled with countless stars, dark dust lanes and glowing gas clouds, and below the Milky Way sits the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that orbits our own.

At Paranal, the Milky Way can shine brightly enough on a dark night to cast shadows of people and objects on the ground. The rosy red clouds are places where stars are forming. Energetic radiation from newborn stars ionizes the hydrogen in the gas and makes it glow.

The VLT, which ESO calls the world's most advanced optical observatory, is made up of four Unit Telescopes, all visible in this photograph, plus four smaller movable Auxiliary Telescopes. One of those appears far off, left of the Unit Telescope in the foreground. Every Unit Telescope has a main mirror 8.2 meters across and can see objects four billion times fainter than the unaided eye can.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no camera or color details.
understand.eye: The eye sees little color in dim light, so the rosy glow of the gas clouds stands out far more in the photograph, even though the Milky Way at Paranal is bright enough to cast shadows.
